entry.title: .NET 10 Release 1: Performance Boosts, Security Upgrades, and Smarter AI
entry.summary:
.NET 10 RC1 is here, and it's a monster. Think your code is fast now? Just wait. The team pulled a Frederic Tudor, the 19th-century "Ice King," compounding thousands of tiny optimizations into a massive performance leap. The JIT is now a wizard at "deabstraction," making your clean, high-level C# run like hand-tuned C.
The real magic trick? Expanded escape analysis. The compiler can now stack-allocate small objects that it proves don't "escape" a method. That means less heap allocation and fewer GC pauses. It's the free performance lunch you were always told doesn't exist. Your app gets faster without you changing a line of code.

If you’ve ever built an AI system that needs to analyze extensive documents or datasets, you’ve probably felt the frustration of watching your API costs skyrocket as you process more and more content.

entry.title: Things That Caught My Attention Last Week - October 3
SQL Server Diagnostics Done Right
entry.summary:
Diagnosing performance issues in SQL Server isn’t guesswork, it’s about using the right data.
In this guide, you’ll learn to collect and interpret live diagnostic signals using DMVs, Query Store. With practical SQL scripts, you’ll see what queries are waiting, who’s blocking, and why tempdb is screaming for help.
Because great diagnostics lead to great fixes.

entry.title: The Overlooked Link Between Security and Performance in SQL Server
entry.summary: Security in SQL Server isn’t just about who can log in, it’s about how queries execute, which context they run under, and how plans are cached. Misconfigured permissions, frequent context switches, and broad user rights silently erode performance. In this article, we’ll explore why secure databases are often faster, what “execution context” really means, and how to fix security-related performance issues one subtle win at a time.

entry.title: Bad Statistics, Bad Execution Plans: The Root of 80% of SQL Server Performance Issues
entry.summary: The SQL Server optimizer doesn’t run your queries, it predicts them. Those predictions depend on statistics and cardinality estimates. When they’re wrong, your query plans explode in cost, memory grants, and row guesses. In this post, we’ll explore how statistics and cardinality estimation shape your query plans, how to spot stale or misleading stats, and how to fix them with code and best practices.

entry.title: Boost Your .NET Projects: Secure Passwords with PBKDF2PasswordHasher in Spargine
entry.summary: The PBKDF2PasswordHasher in Spargine is essential for securely handling passwords in modern applications. It uses the PBKDF2 algorithm to hash passwords with a unique salt and multiple iterations, making it resistant to brute-force attacks. Upcoming updates will enhance its versatility by supporting additional algorithms, ensuring future readiness.

entry.title: Understanding SET XACT_ABORT in SQL Server
entry.summary: Transactions protect your data integrity, but what happens when part of your transaction fails? By default, SQL Server may commit the rest leaving your database inconsistent. In this post, we’ll explore the SET XACT_ABORT setting in SQL Server using the AdventureWorks2022 database, with plenty of examples. You’ll learn why enabling it should be your default for data-modifying stored procedures and scripts.

entry.title: Validating SQL Server Backups
entry.summary: Backups are your last line of defense against data loss but a backup that can’t be restored is worse than no backup at all. In this post, we’ll explore how to validate SQL Server backups using both T-SQL commands and RESTORE VERIFYONLY, how to automate validation checks, and why testing restores regularly is the only real proof of safety. You’ll learn practical scripts, automation strategies, and best practices every DBA should follow.

entry.title: Disk Space is cheap but Bad SQL Design will bankrupt your performance
entry.summary: Many developers shrug off database design issues with one excuse: “Disk space is cheap.” But in SQL Server, inefficiency costs more than gigabytes, it costs I/O, memory, and time. In this article, we’ll explore how oversized datatypes, random GUIDs, and bad clustering choices silently bloat your storage and slow your queries. Through hands-on examples, you’ll see how good schema design saves space, reduces fragmentation, and keeps your SQL Server fast no matter how cheap your disks are.
